Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and approximately one year of data from a comparable instrument at the future Cherenkov Telescope Array site in Chile, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision. This approach yielded a 50 \% improvement for the Auger dataset and a 30 \% improvement for the Chilean dataset. Crucially, this method relies on assuming a VAOD distribution that is both log-normal and isotropic (identical in all directions), an assumption validated by the resulting measurements. Furthermore, this technique functions effectively during bright conditions, operating independently of the sun's exact position, and remains useful even under very dense atmospheric conditions where standard calibration methods struggle due to extremely low signal levels. Given these advantages, this method holds significant potential for deployment at construction sites for new high-energy astrophysics facilities and could be incorporated into their eventual operational systems. In this paper, we detail this method, present its results for two distinct datasets, and conduct an analysis of its uncertainties. Additionally, we demonstrate how a prior estimate of the assumed log-normal VAOD width (standard deviation) can be derived from a short-term time series of oblique imaging photometry captured by a small telescope (15 cm aperture), a strategy that proved effective for both our datasets. Finally, we highlight the method's applicability under very bright viewing conditions, potentially enabling its use during the daytime, provided the telescope field of view is sufficiently narrow to mask the sun's glare.

This study evaluates and compares numerous numerical techniques for addressing stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics, which rely on the Brownian bridge concept for Brownian motion modeling. The proposed method, termed Brownian Bridge Molecular Dynamics (BBMD), represents an innovative advancement over existing approaches. Benchmarks performed on a harmonic oscillator and a model biomolecule demonstrate that BBMD achieves superior accuracy to conventional schemes at equivalent computational costs. Furthermore, BBMD offers the distinct benefit of ensuring positive definite inertia tensor matrices, a property particularly valuable for modeling biomolecules that exhibit internal rotations. Results indicate that the inaccuracy observed in equilateral triangle models using standard methods is primarily due to configurational averaging near degenerate states with inverted inertia tensors, rather than the stochastic integrator itself. Consequently, when restricting dynamics to subspaces with non-inverted inertia tensors, the integrator's precision matches that of BBMD. Given its high accuracy within such restricted dynamics frameworks, BBMD is expected to prove beneficial for molecular dynamics simulations under constraint sampling protocols. As a concluding comparison, it is noted that restricting dynamics yields significantly better configurational averaging than enhanced sampling methods like replica exchange molecular dynamics (REMD), potentially making restricted dynamics with BBMD a viable alternative to REMD for modeling complex biomolecules. Such an approach could serve as a viable substitute for multi-restricted dynamics methods, including REST-2 and ABSOLUTE-SAMPLING. To facilitate broader application, the proposed BBSD and BBMD algorithms are implemented openly via the PyDDM Python package (https://github.com/wulafenyi/pyddm).

Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations. To achieve this, our open-source Python library, FastRoc (recently succeeded by rocast), offers a collection of routines for runcard validation, DNASPD (digital n-spdo) implementations, QCD coupling calculations, and the ROST (rocast output structure) interpolation grids. This article outlines the necessary steps to convert any process provider into the ROST structure via the FastRoc/rocast routines, supplemented by a set of benchmark tests. As a byproduct of these tests, we have identified errors in one existing provider and resolved discrepancies between two providers for the same process. These issues have been corrected in the latest version of CRAPS (http://craps-dafne.infn.it/) following the publication of this article. Our tests also reveal that certain previously used runcard parameters are redundant, as their values can be derived directly from other inputs; consequently, we have established standards for future runcards regarding required parameters, output structures, and the scale. These standards are implemented in the latest rocast version (0.5.0), which serves as the framework for the global fit initiated by the nCTEQ collaboration. Regarding the Virtual Additions to the Neutral Current (VNC) process, which has been included in the most recent experimental dataset for our analysis, we have developed a provider within rocast based on the calculation method described in [1]. Finally, we demonstrate the significance of incorporating the VNC (and potentially other virtual processes) into the global fit, as evidenced by the new dataset added to the nCTEQ-ABQ (nCTEQ17 with Q2 minimum of 0.03 GeV$^2$) global dataset and its subsequent results.
This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing eddy-breakup models proves ineffective for this specific configuration. Consequently, a flame-speed model is utilized instead, demonstrating successful prediction of heat release fluctuations. The linearized active flame model is implemented via a Collocated Boundary Element Method (BEM) for linearization and an Fast Boundary Element Method (FBEM) for solving. BEM offers the advantage of avoiding the linearization of integral representations of turbulence, a step that often introduces significant error. Findings indicate that the linearized active flame model accurately predicts thermoacoustic response modes, aligning well with direct numerical simulation (DNS) results across a range of acoustic drive amplitudes and frequencies. Furthermore, the linear active flame model's predictions of fluctuating velocity and vorticity match the DNS spectral densities at DNS scales. This study confirms that the linear active flame model is a viable and efficient tool for analyzing thermoacoustic instabilities within jet flames, provided an appropriate combustion model is selected. At higher acoustic drive amplitudes, non-linear effects become apparent, warranting further investigation.
Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, circular binary pulsar orbits are employed to constrain the differential constitutive relation, yielding results consistent with those obtained from solar system observations and cosmic scale data. It is also proven that the constitutive relation for NLG cannot remain linear when formulated in terms of measurable variables, a finding that agrees with conclusions drawn from the trace relation and previous constraints based on binary pulsar measurements. Finally, the paper addresses the inversion of the constitutive relation to derive a field equation suitable for initial value problems, a challenge compounded by the fact that the kernel depends on the history of second derivatives. Despite these difficulties, an explicit example of such an inversion is provided.

The survey identifies ten neutron star LMXBs, nine of which exhibit variability; however, no single-source model can account for all observed variability timescales and amplitudes. Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two distinct sets of entities, and their corresponding drawings are widely utilized to visualize these relationships. Our analysis reveals that regularity does not always reduce crossings; specifically, we identify a bipartite graph on $6 \times 6$ vertices that requires fewer crossings in its optimal 2.5-page drawing than in its 2-page drawing. Furthermore, we prove that for any sequence of complete bipartite graphs $K_{n,n}$, the minimum crossings in a $k$-page drawing follow a polynomial relationship with respect to $n$. Finally, we discuss the findings of this work in relation to the convexity of the minimization problem across different drawing methodologies. Additionally, the open issues addressed herein are expected to interest researchers working on multidimensional scaling and heat map visualizations. Notably, we show that minimizing crossings is equivalent to applying a rank-3 approximation, and we establish that the minimum 2.5-page crossing count for a bipartite graph corresponds to the sum of its two largest non-negative eigenvalues from its adjacency matrix. Regarding the concept of crossings, it is important to note that overlaps between edges in a rectangular drawing are mathematically equivalent to crossings in a multidimensional scaling visualization, whereas an edge crossing a column in a heat map visualization aligns with a negative entry in a rank-3 approximation matrix. Ultimately, our findings suggest that regularity remains the most effective strategy for minimizing clutter in heat map visualizations. The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories. Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. Furthermore, the NOVR-XL approach delivers significant sum rate gains over existing VR-based solutions, especially in deployments with large array densities and ultra-high UE densities. To achieve these benefits, UEs should be spaced at least one wavelength apart, a condition easily met in extra-large scale deployments where UE densities are extremely high. Additionally, the proposed solution is vendor-neutral and requires no modifications to existing UE hardware or protocols.
Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield satisfactory results in many scenarios, effectively capturing significant linguistic knowledge at a low computational cost. Leveraging this insight, we propose training a neural model to predict the residuals between an $N$-gram model and the actual data distribution. This hybrid approach enables the neural component to concentrate on deeper linguistic understanding while offering a flexible framework for customization; one can switch the underlying $N$-gram model without retraining the neural component. Experiments across three standard tasks—language modeling, machine translation, and summarization—consistently show that our method outperforms existing standalone neural models. Furthermore, the approach facilitates effective domain adaptation by simply swapping in a domain-specific $N$-gram model, requiring no additional training. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.
This study introduces Informed OCR, a system designed to correct the errors produced by conventional OCR when processing the output of earlier runs of Informed OCR itself. This creates a recursive workflow where multiple iterations of Informed OCR can be executed in a pipeline to progressively enhance the quality of the final results. The framework integrates the error models of two distinct OCR engines, Tesseract and a neural network-based engine, Abysmal, to guide a search algorithm that explores a lattice of hypothesized character corrections. We evaluated this approach using a real-world dataset of historically degraded legal judgments that had been OCR'd twice with poor results using Tesseract. The findings indicate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art error correction techniques, achieving significant improvements in character-level accuracy (by 19.4 percentage points) and string-level precision (by 11.4 percentage points) on the ICDT dataset. Furthermore, the results confirm that employing a pipeline of recursive Informed OCR runs yields progressively better character-level recognition accuracy compared to using a single conventional OCR run. The source code and the dataset for Informed OCR are publicly accessible at https://informed-ocr.com.
This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere. The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. The progression of circulation regimes with respect to the planetary rotation rate aligns qualitatively with predictions from theoretical rotating flow models. By defining non-dimensional scales for horizontal length, angular velocity, and vertical velocity, distinct regimes are characterized based on dominant physical processes and length-scale preferences. An Earth's atmospheric GCM was employed to delineate rotation-rate regimes, revealing that for current Earth parameters, the dominant regime is a multiple-jet flow. While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at addressing large-scale problems across numerous domains, their deployment in real-time systems is often hindered by the sheer volume of parameters involved. To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were initially introduced in the context of knowledge distillation, enabling lightweight student networks to match the performance of complex teacher models. Recently, these architectures have been widely adopted for diverse knowledge learning tasks, including knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Leveraging such frameworks, recent research has successfully achieved multiple learning objectives through efficient and compact student networks. Unlike previous surveys focused solely on knowledge distillation, this review comprehensively examines Teacher-Student architectures across a spectrum of knowledge learning goals. Furthermore, we systematically outline the processes of knowledge construction and optimization, analyze various architectural designs and learning strategies used to acquire representative and robust knowledge, and summarize recent applications in classification, recognition, and generation. Finally, we explore future research directions concerning architecture design, knowledge quality, and theoretical advancements in regression-based learning. By providing a thorough overview, this survey offers valuable insights and practical guidelines for both industry professionals and the academic community regarding Teacher-Student architectures in multi-objective knowledge learning. Moreover, the provided architecture diagrams and flowcharts serve as useful resources for new entries. The complete survey can be accessed at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01525.
We introduce a new, compact representation for graphical models, a foundational framework for numerous reasoning tasks. Leveraging deterministic finite state automata, we integrate this concise representation into Bucket Elimination (BE), a general variable elimination method used for inference and optimization problems like most probable explanation and constrained optimization. We refer to this enhanced approach as FABE. Incorporating our compact representation into FABE significantly enhances BE's performance regarding both runtime and memory usage. Empirical comparisons between FABE and leading methods for most probable explanation (recursive best-first, structured message passing) and constrained optimization (CPLEX, GUROBI, toulbar2), conducted via a standard methodology, validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating runtime gains of up to five orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we assessed FABE's efficacy in a visual grounding application, where it outperformed existing solutions in runtime on a benchmark designed to identify objects in autonomous vehicle scenarios. Finally, we discuss how this representation can facilitate the construction of large-scale graphical model specifications. As the representation becomes more compact, it may enable the construction of previously infeasible graphical models. Our open-source implementation of FABE is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/hiro-fuc/tnt.
The recently introduced higher rank Racah algebra $R(n)$ is reviewed, followed by the definition of a quotient algebra by central elements termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$. Leveraging classical invariant theory, it is demonstrated that $sR(n)$ is isomorphic to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ corresponding to the diagonal embedding of $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)^{\otimes n}$. This isomorphism yields a new presentation of $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ via generators and relations. Furthermore, an explicit Hilbert-Poincar\'e series is derived and analyzed, with the implications of these findings extended to the special Askey-Wilson algebra and its higher rank variants. Finally, the connection between $R(n)$ and a family of non-commutative homogeneous polynomials previously identified and studied by the authors is reviewed. The utility of this polynomial family in deriving an explicit formula for the Harish-Chandra isomorphism for $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ beyond the special level 2 is also discussed. Potential applications to establishing Hilbert-Poincar\'e series for higher rank Racah algebras and their relation to the polynomial family of Fein, Lemmon, and Saidak are briefly considered. Potential links to quantum affine algebra centralizers and tensor decompositions are also outlined. Notably, the proof relying on invariant theory utilized here to establish the isomorphism between $r(n)$ and $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2}$ at generic $q$ (and consequently for $r(n)$) relies on the fact that two non-zero classical invariant theory elements sharing the same degree and rank are isomorphic; extending this proof to integer values of $q$ would demand an explicit isomorphism between specific generators of $R(n)$ and $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ at $q=1$, a challenge acknowledged but not resolved in this work. Finally, the utility of invariant theory in addressing similar problems within the recently defined higher rank Askey-Wilson algebra is explored. Potential applications to finding Hilbert-Poincar\'e series for the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$ and its relation to the polynomial family of Fein, Lemmon, and Saidak are also discussed.
Significance testing, particularly the paired-permutation test, has been essential for ensuring that performance differences between NLP systems are statistically significant rather than due to chance. However, practitioners have historically relied on Monte Carlo approximations because no suitable exact algorithm existed. This paper introduces an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test applicable to a specific family of structured test statistics. The proposed algorithm operates in $\mathcal{O}(GN (\log GN )(\log N ))$ time, where $N$ represents the dataset size and $G$ denotes the range of the test statistic. Experimental results indicate that our exact algorithm is 10 times faster than a Monte Carlo approximation using 20,000 samples on a standard dataset. Furthermore, the algorithm scales effectively to large datasets, achieving speedups of over 100 compared to Monte Carlo methods with identical significance levels. These findings suggest that the exact algorithm can be practically employed on large datasets to conduct more rigorous hypotheses tests than currently feasible. To facilitate broader usage, the exact algorithm and a related confidence interval algorithm are available as a free C++ library and as an API on GitHub at https://github.com/TechNLP/EatMR.
Using the AMPT multiphase transport model, we investigated the connection between initial geometric anisotropy and anisotropic flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Our results show that, unlike the elliptic flow $v_2$, the triangular flow $v_3$ exhibits minimal dependence on centrality. Once the influence of initial geometry is accounted for, the ratio $v_3/\epsilon_3$ rises with increasing transverse particle density, mirroring the behavior of $v_2/\epsilon_2$. Furthermore, the $p_T$ dependence of $v_3$ observed across identified particles follows a qualitative pattern similar to that of $v_2$. These trends are consistently reproduced in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, suggesting that partonic interactions and subsequent hydrodynamical responses drive this phenomenon. These findings imply that the generation of triangular anisotropy in the initial state and the corresponding anisotropic flow can be treated as uncorrelated phenomena, independent of the specific heavy ion system or collision centrality.
This study presents a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that models target birth and undetected target intensities on a grid. It employs a simplified Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter to predict undetected target intensities and approximates the density of first-time detections using Gaussian distributions. Unlike traditional PMBM implementations that rely on Gaussian mixtures to represent undetected target intensities, this approach enables the intensity to change across the region of interest with sharp transitions at the sensor's field of view, avoiding the need for numerous Gaussian mixture components. Consequently, this method lowers computational complexity compared to conventional techniques. The proposed technique is demonstrated within a sensor management framework, where sensor trajectories with restricted fields of view are optimized to search for and track targets within a specific area. Simulation results validate the effectiveness of this approach and highlight its benefits over conventional methods. These findings suggest that combining a sensor's point-like characteristics with a grid-based representation for the undetected target intensity is more appropriate than assuming a Gaussian distribution, particularly when the sensor has a narrow field of view and the probability of the target being outside the sensor's view is high. These conclusions are not limited to the specific sensor model or estimation method used here but apply broadly to similar configurations. Furthermore, the approach of modeling the undetected target intensity with a peak at the sensor's location offers a clear physical interpretation, facilitating the incorporation of prior information regarding the target's most likely position.
Soccer is a game characterized by sparse rewards, where even intelligent or negligent decisions in pivotal moments can alter the match outcome. Consequently, players, coaches, and scouts seek to identify the optimal actions during critical phases, such as high-risk scenarios involving potential loss of possession or scoring opportunities. This study introduces a novel state representation for soccer combined with batch reinforcement learning to train a policy network capable of determining the best action. By processing contextual information, the network aims to maximize the team's expected goals. Extensive numerical experiments were conducted using InStat logs covering 104 European matches, demonstrating that the optimized policy consistently achieved higher rewards than the behavior policy across all games. Furthermore, the learned policies align closely with real-world behaviors; for instance, the optimized policy reveals that in specific contexts, actions like fouling or kicking the ball out can yield greater rewards than taking a shot. These findings offer valuable insights for coaches and players regarding the most effective behaviors in various situations. Additionally, the approach demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, as the optimized policy derived from a single dataset successfully performed well on a completely different dataset. This work represents the first application of batch reinforcement learning to soccer, utilizing a contextual state space. Future research could explore state spaces incorporating more dynamic contextual elements and investigate advanced optimized network architectures, such as context-aware networks, to further improve performance. Moreover, the methods developed here have the potential to be adapted for other sports data challenges.

At colliders, neutral long-lived particles are identified either via displaced decay products or as missing energy, with the optimal search strategy depending on both the detector characteristics and the particle's decay length. This study examines the complementary nature of these signatures for the Belle II experiment, specifically focusing on axion-like particles ($a$) generated from meson decays. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $B^+ \to K^+ a$ followed by $a\to E\!\!\!/$, where $E\!\!\!/$ represents missing energy. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $50\,$ab$^{-1}$, Belle II is capable of probing light invisible resonances with branching ratios $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) \gtrsim 10^{-7}$ and decay lengths $c\tau_a \gtrsim 1\,$m. For axion-like particles, we anticipate that the sensitivity of the $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ channel to small couplings could improve by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior searches at fixed-target and collider facilities. Specifically, for sub-GeV particles, the combination of $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ at Belle II and beam-dump experiments offers the greatest sensitivity, whereas for heavier particles, the smallest couplings can be probed through displaced vertex searches at Belle II, long-lived particle studies at the LHC, and future fixed-target experiments. We also provide saddle-point contours illustrating the optimal global search strategies across a wide mass range for both axion-like and dark photon particles. Furthermore, we detail the analysis capabilities required at Belle II to distinguish between resonant signatures from long-lived particle decays and non-resonant sources such as semi-visible jets originating from dark QCD. Finally, we discuss the potential of these searches to uncover decay chains that enable dark sector candidates to account for the dark matter abundance. The analysis framework presented here can be applied to diverse dark sector models and at various experimental facilities. To facilitate this, we have developed \texttt{LLVv2}, an upgraded version of the lightweight analysis tool \texttt{LLV} designed for missing-energy searches at colliders, which is available on GitHub at \url{https://github.com/belle-ii/LLVv2}.
This paper offers a qualitative examination of potentially flawed outputs generated by contextualized embedding-based techniques for identifying diachronic semantic change. We first introduce an ensemble method that surpasses prior contextualized approaches, which then serves as the foundation for a detailed analysis of predicted semantic shifts in English vocabulary over five decades. Our results indicate that these methods frequently assign high change scores to words that are not actually undergoing genuine diachronic semantic shifts, or where the validity of such shifts is dubious. We provide detailed discussions of these challenging instances with specific examples and propose corresponding linguistic classifications. Ultimately, we conclude that pre-trained contextualized language models tend to conflate changes in lexicographic senses with variations in contextual frequency, a bias inherent to their distributional nature that differs from issues seen in static embedding methods. Furthermore, these models often blend syntactic and semantic features of lexical items. Finally, we suggest several potential future solutions to address these problems. To facilitate this investigation, we release a comprehensive dataset of English words across five time periods (1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2009) with vector representations from multiple contextualized embedding methods, along with a detailed examination of difficult cases at https://github.com/Alexisambores/DSCC. Our findings should be especially relevant to researchers utilizing these methods to investigate lexical variation across languages or dialects, or when exploring vocabulary shifts over time. Additionally, this study will be of interest to those developing methods to identify diachronic semantic change and developing algorithms for related tasks. As a byproduct of this analysis, we inadvertently address a concern regarding the utility of contextualized embeddings for measuring text importance or relevance; our data shows that methods like BERT assign similar importance to words regardless of their parent text, a characteristic shared by other contextualized approaches. Conversely, our dataset confirms that static contextualized embeddings, such as FastText-crfc and FastText-char, remain effective at capturing lexical variation across corpora and distinguishing lexicographic senses, a capability absent in BERT. These findings regarding static methods align with earlier research (Rudolph et al., 2019; Pamula et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020), whereas the limitations observed for BERT are novel. Our dataset will also prove valuable for future research aiming to understand the characteristics of contextualized embeddings and their applications.
The masses and spins of black holes powering Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) and producing jets can be investigated through their electromagnetic spectra. We employ the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear relationship linking four source-frame variables: radio luminosity, X-ray or optical luminosity (derived from the [OIII] emission line), black hole mass, and spin. By incorporating uncertainties related to luminosity measurements, conversion factors, relativistic beaming, and AGN physical properties, we establish lower limits on the spins of a sample of massive, jetted AGNs. Utilizing these findings, we examine the direct consequences for the mass spectrum of ultra-light scalar (axion-like), vector (dark photon), and tensor (additional spin-2) particles, specifically addressing the previously unexplored parameter range of $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Considering that self-interactions might inhibit axion instability and explain the lack of observed superradiance, we derive upper limits on the axion decay constant (which correspond to lower limits on self-interaction strength). Furthermore, assuming axions are defined by mass and decay constant, we determine the maximum fraction of dark matter attributable to ultra-light particles, concluding that a single species of axion-like particle can account for no more than $10\%$ of dark matter within the mass interval $10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$. Finally, we discuss the implications of these upper limits on self-interaction for axion dominance in the sector of multi-component ultra-light dark matter. To facilitate future research, we provide public access to the data underpinning this study at https://github.com/EmmanouilPapoutsakis/MassSpinUncertainties and to the code used to derive axion limits in the face of self-interaction via http://doi.org/10.21100/axcaps.v1.

We simulated the ground states of quantum harmonic oscillators subjected to either constant forces of varying magnitudes or time-dependent driving forces. Expectation values of position were computed for different combinations of mass, natural angular frequency, and the coupling constant $\lambda$ under both driving conditions. Under constant forcing, the simulations yielded coherent states. The outcomes for both scenarios align almost perfectly with theoretical predictions. To perform these simulations, we implemented the Metropolis algorithm on a discrete time lattice to evaluate the systems' imaginary time path integrals. This approach offers significant advantages for finding ground states of quantum many-body systems under constant or time-dependent driving, particularly in regimes where wave function sampling methods struggle due to the "sign problem." Additionally, this real-space methodology is easily adaptable to higher dimensions and can handle complex geometries and boundary conditions.
We introduce a variant of the quantum relational Hoare logic from Unruh (POPL 2019) that incorporates "expectations" into pre- and postconditions. Specifically, when reasoning about pairs of programs, this logic enables quantitative analysis of the degree to which pre- and postconditions regarding the relationship between program inputs and outputs are satisfied. To achieve this, we utilize a semantics for reasoning over relations composed of states and expectations. Furthermore, we conduct soundness and completeness proofs demonstrating that the soundness of inference rules relies on the fact that non-zero expectations are distributed linearly, whereas completeness is achieved by considering the linearity of both states and expectations. Finally, we apply this enhanced quantum relational Hoare logic to derive sound specifications for a broader range of quantum libraries and constructs than previously possible with the original formulation. These constructs include controlled operations, the quantum if construct, uniform and clean measurement constructs, and quantum while loops. As a practical implementation, we have developed a tool called Qhare-C, which is an SHAPER-based extractor of relational invariants capable of proving equality relations and now, with our approach, proofs involving invariants based on expectations. The source code for Qhare-C, alongside a collection of examples, is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/mharrtmr/Qhare-C. By utilizing these examples, we illustrate how our method facilitates the quantitative reasoning about performance regarding work and entropy cost constructs.
This study addresses the bias—defined as over- or underestimation—in the line-of-sight perpendicular component ($B_{\perp}$) of vector magnetic field maps. While prior research has established the existence of this issue, our work conducts novel investigations to quantify the bias, identify its root causes, and propose mitigation strategies. First, we establish quantitative metrics to measure $B_{\perp}$ bias across both local physical components and native image-plane components. Second, we systematically evaluate various inversion methods and data sources, explicitly accounting for the magnetic field's geometry and the instrument's physical configuration. Our results indicate that the bias stems from two primary factors: the geometric relationship between the line-of-sight and the image plane, and the anisotropy in the magnetic field distribution. Consequently, we demonstrate that simple tilting the estimator or utilizing a different inversion method cannot fully resolve the problem. Finally, we introduce a rigorous mapping of the field geometry onto the image plane as a mitigation approach; when combined with polarimetric inversion, this method significantly reduces the bias. To validate these findings, we applied these techniques to real solar observations, comparing the outcomes with those from the 15-minute magnetogram workflow used by Solar-Geophysical Alerts and nowcast systems. As a concluding recommendation, we advocate for explicitly incorporating the line-of-sight component into the metadata of vector magnetic field maps. Furthermore, we provide Python codes for calculating the geometric relationship and assessing bias, available at https://github.com/tommasoabbot/ComponentPerpBias.
For a Coxeter system $(W,S)$, we define the boolean complex of involutions as a counterpart to the boolean complex of $W$ investigated by Ragnarsson and Tenner. Utilizing discrete Morse theory, we establish the homotopy type of this complex for a broad range of $(W,S)$, specifically covering all finite Coxeter groups, revealing that it corresponds to a wedge of spheres with dimension $|S| - 1$. Furthermore, we derive straightforward recurrence relations to calculate the number of spheres comprising this wedge. Applying these recurrence relations, we explicitly determine the homotopy type of the boolean complex of involutions for the affine Weyl groups associated with $A_2$, $A_3$, and $A_4$. Additionally, for any integer $n \geq 2$, we demonstrate that the $(n+2)$-dimensional boolean complex of involutions for the affine Weyl group corresponding to $A_n$ is contractible. These findings extend the results previously detailed by Ragnarsson and Tenner regarding the boolean complex of involutions for classical groups. As a corollary, we revisit the recurrence relations governing the enumeration of involutions within $(W,S)$. The introduction of the boolean complex of involutions for $(W,S)$ serves as the foundation for this study. Moreover, given a set $X$ and a function $f: \mathcal{P}(X) \to \mathcal{P}(X)$, we generalize this definition to construct a boolean complex associated with $(W,S)$ and a pair of functions $(f,g)$, analyzing its fundamental properties. Finally, we examine these complexes for the symmetric groups $S_n$ and the groups $S_n \times S_n$.
This paper establishes that no special timelike Frenet curve constitutes a Bertrand curve in $\mathbb{E}_2^4$, and in $\mathbb{E}_\nu^{n+1}$ for $n \ge 3$, the concept of a Bertrand curve is strictly defined only within $\mathbb{E}_1^2$ and $\mathbb{E}_1^3$. Consequently, a generalization termed the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve is introduced for $\mathbb{E}_2^4$, alongside a detailed characterization of this curve type within the same space. Additionally, the implications of a timelike (1,4)-Bertrand curve in $\mathbb{E}_2^4$ are discussed. The study of varieties of timelike (1, $n$)-Bertrand curves in $\mathbb{E}_2^{n+1}$ where $n \ge 4$ is also briefly addressed. Consequently, varieties of regular variety Bertrand curves in $\mathbb{E}_a^b$ are defined and their properties examined. Finally, varieties of timelike (1, $n$)-Bertrand curves in $\mathbb{E}_1^{n+1}$ are defined and their characteristics investigated. In varieties of Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{E}^{n+1}$, the existence of regular variety Bertrand curves is fully characterized.
Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. To facilitate this, we introduce a unified framework capable of testing any loss function across diverse datasets, ensuring compatibility with state-of-the-art methodologies.
We introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of everyday commonsense reasoning structured through 877,000 textual descriptions of inferential knowledge. Unlike existing resources that primarily focus on taxonomic information, our emphasis is inferential. To facilitate the efficient retrieval of diverse inferential knowledge, we have developed a modular labeling system using a broad spectrum of inferential relations. This approach allows for the annotation of various forms of commonsense entailment as simple binary relations between these labels. To enable rapid access to both knowable relations and their instances, we have constructed a hierarchical graph that connects instances, typological relations, and inferential relations. Agents can utilize this abundant commonsense knowledge for tasks such as language understanding and inference. To ensure the consistency of inferential relations with instance contexts, we trained a neural network classifier on the instance-context-relation triples in our atlas. This network can identify contexts where specified inferential relations are unsupportable, effectively acting as a "reality check" for textual contexts. Agents can leverage this capability as a "commonsense reality check" for contexts they are uncertain about regarding their commonsense validity. Access to the ATOMIC atlas, including a API for retrieving instances, typological relations, and inferential relations for specific instances, is available at http://atomic.ai2-semantics.org/. To explore the instances and inferential relations within the atlas, please visit http://atoms.explorecommonsense.com/. Our work aligns with the vision of a "commonsense revolution" (Muggleton, 2006; Sabel and Muggleton, 2009; Muggleton, 2010, 2012; Mascarilla et al., 2013; Muggleton, 2014), which advocates for integrating artificial intelligence with psychology and sociology to create intelligent agents capable of reasoning about common sense akin to humans. Furthermore, our resource supports linguistic research by providing resources for semantic analysis and addressing linguistic gaps, similar to initiatives like WordNet (Miller, 1995), iSemantics (Mascarilla et al., 2013), and Pelletier et al. (2013). Finally, our resource contributes to cognitive science by offering resources for studying inferential commonsense knowledge, comparable to resources like PRIME-TIME (Haldar et al., 2016) and COPES (Madhavan et al., 2016).
This work tackles novel view video prediction, where a network generates video from an unseen angle based on input clips from one or multiple existing views. Unlike recent methods that handle only minor viewpoint shifts, our prior-free approach successfully predicts videos across wider angular ranges, up to 45 degrees. Furthermore, the method utilizes solely RGB frames to learn a dual representation comprising both view-dependent and global components; the latter integrates complementary details to facilitate prediction from novel viewpoints. We validate the framework's efficacy on two real-world datasets, NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic. Comparative analysis against state-of-the-art techniques reveals significant improvements without relying on explicit priors from target views: a 26.1% gain in SSIM, a 13.6% increase in PSNR, and a 60% reduction in FVD scores. Additionally, the model can be applied to generate videos for views never seen during training. Finally, the approach scales effectively to multiple source views to enhance prediction quality from novel views, potentially enabling systems like omnidirectional video prediction. Our method builds upon a Transformer architecture, recently shown to perform well in visual tasks, adapted here for novel view video prediction. This study reports the potential detection of a nonmonotonic radial rotation profile in a low-mass, low-luminosity giant star. When applied to the smaller WikiMovies dataset, our method achieved a threefold increase in exact match scores on the MetaQA task relative to the T5 baseline. When X-rays strike the mirror segments, they are directed by the LE effect onto the common sensor. To map the directions of X-rays hitting the mirror segments onto the shared sensor, we employed tomographic reconstruction methods. Using a 30-segment MuLE configuration, a previous study demonstrated that a 2D wide-field X-ray monitor could be built with 30 mirror segments and just two image sensors (charge-coupled devices), covering a 2.4 sr field of view (FoV). Our findings indicate that four mirror segments and three sensors can achieve a 4$\pi$-sr FoV, while a configuration of ten segments and three sensors can cover approximately 99.9% of the sky. These results suggest that constructing a wide-field X-ray monitor with a 4$\pi$-sr FoV via MuLE optics is feasible and potentially beneficial for a future generation of X-ray monitors. We present an implementation of a deep learning framework designed to explore dark matter structure formation. Our approach involves training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshots of a dark matter-only simulation to forecast the halo mass into which individual particles will collapse by $z=0$, within a range determined by the initial power spectrum. While the CNN successfully mapped particle characteristics to their final halo masses, it also uncovered that velocity field information yields negligible improvements in predictions when the initial power spectrum is "standard," but offers substantial advantages when the spectrum is "tilted." Furthermore, we demonstrate that inclusion-exclusion net (INCNET) layers can effectively integrate features derived from both the density and velocity fields, resulting in significant performance gains over models relying on a single input source. These findings are particularly evident in simulations with a tilted power spectrum, guiding the optimal design of convolutional neural network architectures for cosmological studies across different power spectrum configurations. Notably, our models require no training on the actual $N$-body simulation data, as the CNN's ability to learn from particle characteristics (density and velocity) alone is sufficient for this specific cosmological scenario. To access additional physical parameters, such as cosmological models or simulation specifics, fully connected layers can be added to the network's final stages. Our results indicate that convolutional neural networks are particularly effective when the information being learned is spatially localized, a concept we visualize using a tomographic image of the linear power spectrum. Ultimately, we conclude that the halo mass function is fundamentally driven by the initial power spectrum rather than the underlying simulation box size. Detecting the magnetic field expelled by a superconductor through spatial resolution remains a significant experimental challenge. In this study, we detail the detection of the London Moment LM ($\omega_L$) by a 1$mu$Bi (monolayer bismuth) film positioned above its critical temperature transition Tc using an AC SQUID (Superconducting Quantum Interference Device) as the sensing element. Our results demonstrate that the LM origin is not the Meissner Effect (ME), which expels the magnetic field, but rather the screening of an already present internal magnetic field. This screening occurs via persistent eddy currents induced within the superconducting material. Consequently, the London Moment should be observable in normal state materials that exhibit the Meissner Effect, such as lead (Pb) and aluminum (Al), yet it is not. Furthermore, our data indicate that the magnetic flux penetrating the 1$mu$Bi film during the transition from the normal to the superconducting state is independent of the applied external magnetic field. Finally, we find that the screening of the London Moment in our sample is unrelated to the flux exclusion characteristic of the ME. To address these findings, we propose a two-component order parameter model for the London Moment.

While optimizing chassis and body construction can mitigate these issues, it often leads to increased costs and extended development cycles. Introducing a source term into the governing equations offers an effective post-factum solution. This paper investigates the inverse problem of reconstructing such a source term. This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. Furthermore, we confirm that the consistency of direct detection with the relic density depends on the specific mass of the median dark matter partner.
